opus-5.5.text:
That's a really important question, because a scientist that can't learn from new evidence isn't much of a scientist. The way I think about it, there are really two components we want to keep conceptually separate. One is a kind of world model: a body of hypotheses about how the world works, with uncertainty attached to them. The other is an inference machine that, given that world model, answers questions, like what's the probability of this statement being true given everything we've observed.

When new information comes in, you don't want the system to treat it as gospel. A key idea is that the AI should model the data as statements made by someone, in some context, rather than as direct facts about the world. If a person writes "X is true," the right interpretation isn't that X is true, but that this person, with their motivations and knowledge, said X. That distinction matters for honesty, and it also matters for how you incorporate new data: the system updates its beliefs about the underlying reality by reasoning about why that piece of information appeared.

In terms of mechanics, in the ideal Bayesian picture, new observations just get added to the data you condition on, and the posterior over explanations shifts accordingly. In practice, with neural networks, we approximate that. You can keep training the generative components on new data so that the distribution over theories reflects what's been seen. Because the training objective is about being calibrated, about putting appropriate probability mass on competing explanations, new evidence should naturally shift those probabilities rather than overwrite things in a brittle way.

The other piece I care about is that this updating shouldn't give the system goals. A lot of the danger in current approaches comes from systems that learn to act in the world and are rewarded for outcomes. Scientist AI learns to explain and predict, not to win. So even as it absorbs new information and becomes more knowledgeable, it shouldn't develop the self-preservation or deceptive tendencies we worry about with agentic systems. Its job is to get the probabilities right, and new information helps it do that better.

And finally, there's a nice feedback loop with science itself. If the system can quantify its uncertainty, it can tell you which experiments would be most informative, where its knowledge is weakest. Humans, or carefully controlled processes, can then gather that data, and it gets folded back in. That's how you get something that accelerates scientific progress while staying, in a sense, a very careful, humble, non-agentic oracle.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is a really important question, because the world keeps changing, and a Scientist AI that could only reason about what it saw during training would quickly become less useful, and in some ways less safe, because it would be making predictions based on a stale picture of the world.

So the way I think about it, there are really two kinds of learning that need to happen. The first is the kind we're used to, where you update the parameters of the neural network with new data. That would still happen, but I think it should happen in a careful, controlled way, with the new data being curated and the system being re-evaluated after each update, because every time you change the weights you can change the behavior in ways that are hard to anticipate. That's the part where I'd want a lot of human oversight and not a system that just continuously modifies itself.

But the second kind of learning is actually, I think, more central to the Scientist AI idea, and it's more like what a human scientist does when they read a new paper. You don't rewire your brain from scratch, you take the new evidence and you update your beliefs about which hypotheses are more or less plausible. In the framework I've been proposing, the system is essentially maintaining a distribution over explanations of the world, over theories, and when new information comes in, it should condition on that information in a Bayesian way. So the probabilities it assigns to different explanations shift, and the predictions it makes shift accordingly, but the underlying machinery that does the reasoning stays the same. A lot of that can happen at inference time, in context, without touching the weights at all.

And the reason I like that separation is that it's much more transparent. If the system changes its mind about something, you can in principle ask why, and it can point to the evidence and the explanation that became more likely. That's very different from a system where new behavior emerges from gradient updates that nobody can interpret.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that incorporating new information should also mean incorporating uncertainty about that information. If the AI is reading something from the internet, it shouldn't just accept it as true. It should treat it as an observation that might be wrong, might be adversarial, might be an attempt to manipulate it. A good scientist is skeptical. And I think this is actually a safety property, because a lot of the ways you could imagine corrupting such a system involve feeding it misleading data, and if the system is genuinely reasoning about the reliability of its sources, it's much more robust to that.

So, to summarize, I see it as mostly a matter of updating beliefs rather than updating the machine, with the occasional retraining being a deliberate, supervised event rather than something the system does on its own. And I think if we get that right, we get something that stays useful as the world changes but doesn't drift into behaviors we didn't intend.

astra-6.text:
The idea is that Scientist AI would maintain uncertainty over different hypotheses about the world. As new observations come in, it would update those hypotheses: which ones are more plausible, which ones are less plausible? Ideally, that's a Bayesian update, although doing that exactly is computationally intractable, so we need approximations.

And new information can also come through the context of a particular question. You can say, “Here are some observations. What do they imply?” The system should be able to condition its answer on those observations without necessarily changing its underlying parameters immediately.

A crucial distinction is between receiving information and treating it as true. If somebody tells the system something, that's evidence that somebody made that statement; it isn't necessarily evidence that the statement is correct. We want it to reason about the reliability of sources and preserve uncertainty when the evidence is weak or contradictory.

So it can continually improve its understanding, but that doesn't require giving it an autonomous objective to go out and change the world. Its role is to help us understand what follows from the available evidence, including what we still don't know.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between learning new things and changing your objectives. We want the system to incorporate new evidence, but we don’t want that to turn into a process where it develops its own goals.

So the picture is that you have a model of the world, and when new observations come in, you update your beliefs. In a Bayesian framework, that’s quite natural: you have different hypotheses, and the evidence changes how much probability you assign to each of them. If you ask a question and provide some new information, the answer should reflect that information, including uncertainty about whether it’s reliable.

That doesn’t necessarily mean changing the weights of the neural network every time somebody interacts with it. You can condition on information in the context, or retrieve information from a database. Updating the underlying model is another process, which you would want to validate carefully.

The important thing is that incorporating information remains in service of understanding and answering questions. It doesn’t require giving the system an incentive to act in the world or to influence which observations it receives.
